source_text: Ποῖον οὐ νικῶσι θηρίον τῇ χαλεπότητι τῶν τρόπων; Τί τῶν ἀνημέρων οὐχ ὑπερ βάλλουσιν ἀγριότητι; Οἱ κύνες τρεφόμενοι ἡμεροῦν ται· οἱ λέοντες χειροήθεις γίνονται θεραπευόμενοι· οἱ δὲ βάσκανοι ταῖς θεραπείαις πλέον ἐξαγριαί νονται. Τί τὸν γενναῖον Ἰωσὴφ δοῦλον ἐποίησεν; Οὐχ ὁ φθόνος τῶν ἀδελφῶν; Ἔνθα καὶ θαυμάσαι ἄξιον τὴν ἀλογίαν τῆς νόσου. Φοβηθέντες γὰρ τῶν ὀνειράτων τὴν ἔκβασιν, δοῦλον ἐποίουν τὸν ἀδελφὸν, ὡς οὐκ ἄν ποτε δούλου προσκυνηθέντος. Καίτοι εἰ μὲν ἀληθῆ τὰ ἐνύπνια, τίς μηχανὴ μὴ οὐχὶ πάντως ἐκβῆναι τὰ προῤῥηθέντα; εἰ δὲ ψευδεῖς αἱ τῶν ὀνειράτων ὄψεις, ἀντὶ τίνος βασκαίνετε τῷ σφαλλομένῳ; Νυνὶ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ οἰκονομίας περιτρέπεται αὐτοῖς τὸ σοφόν. Δι' ὧν γὰρ ἐνόμιζον ἐμποδίζειν τῇ προῤῥήσει, διὰ τούτων ἐφάνησαν ὁδο ποιοῦντες τὴν ἔκβασιν. Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἐπράθη, οὐκ ἂν ἦλθεν εἰς Αἴγυπτον, οὐκ ἂν διὰ σωφροσύνην ταῖς ἐπιβουλαῖς τῆς ἀκολάστου γυναικὸς περιέπεσεν, οὐκ ἂν ἐβλήθη εἰς δεσμωτήριον, οὐκ ἂν ἐγένετο συνήθης τοῖς ὑπηρέταις τοῦ Φαραὼ, οὐδ' ἂν συνέβαλε τὰ ὀνείρατα, ὅθεν τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐδέξατο τῆς Αἰγύπτου, καὶ διὰ τὴν σιτοδείαν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀδελφῶν αὐτοῦ πρὸς αὐ τὸν ἐλθόντων προσεκυνήθη. Μετάβα τῷ λόγῳ ἐπὶ τὸν μέγιστον φθόνον, καὶ ἐπὶ μεγίστοις συστάντα, ὃς ἐκ τῆς Ἰουδαίων μανίας κατὰ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἐγέ νετο. Διὰ τί ἐφθονεῖτο; Διὰ τὰ θαύματα. Τίνες δὲ ἦσαν αἱ θαυματοποιίαι; Σωτηρία τῶν δεομένων· ἐτρέφοντο οἱ πεινῶντες, καὶ ὁ τρέφων ἐπολεμεῖτο· ἠγείροντο οἱ νεκροὶ, καὶ ὁ ζωοποιῶν ἐβασκαίνετο· δαίμονες ἀπηλαύνοντο, καὶ ὁ ἐπιτάσσων ἐπεβουλεύετο· λεπροὶ ἐκαθαρίζοντο, καὶ χωλοὶ περιεπάτουν, κωφοὶ ἤκουον, καὶ τυφλοὶ ἀνέβλεπον, καὶ ὁ εὐεργέτης ἐφυγαδεύετο. Καὶ τὸ τελευταῖον θανάτῳ παρέδωκαν τὸν τὴν ζωὴν χαρισάμενον, καὶ ἐμαστί γουν τὸν ἐλευθερωτὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ κατεδίκαζον τὸν κριτὴν τοῦ κόσμου. Οὕτω μέχρι πάντων διεξῆλθε τὰ τοῦ φθόνου κακά. Καὶ ἑνὶ τούτῳ ὅπλῳ ἀπὸ καταβολῆς ἀρξάμενος κόσμου μέχρι συν τελείας αἰῶνος πάντας τιτρώσκει καὶ καταβάλλει ὁ λυμεὼν τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν διάβολος, ὁ χαίρων ἡμῶν τῇ ἀπωλείᾳ, ὁ καταπεσὼν διὰ τοῦ φθόνου, καὶ ἡμᾶς ἑαυτῷ διὰ τοῦ ἴσου πάθους συγκαταβάλλων. Σοφὸς ἄρα ἦν ὁ τῷ βασκάνῳ ἀνδρὶ μηδὲ συνδειπνεῖν ἐπιτρέπων· ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν τῷ δείπνῳ συνουσίας περὶ πάσης ὁμοῦ τῆς κατὰ τὸν βίον κοινωνίας διαλεγόμενος. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὴν εὐκατάπρηστον ὕλην ἐπιμελὲς ἡμῖν ὅτι ποῤῥωτάτω τοῦ πυρὸς ἀποτίθεσθαι, οὕτω χρὴ, καθ' ὅσον οἷόν τε, τῆς τῶν βασκάνων ὁμιλίας τὰς φιλίας ἀπάγειν, ἔξω τῶν τοῦ φθόνου βελῶν ἑαυ τοὺς ποιοῦντας. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄλλως δυνατὸν συμπλακῆναι τῷ φθόνῳ, μὴ δι' οἰκειότητος αὐτῷ προσεγγίσαντα. Ἐπείπερ κατὰ τὸν Σολομῶντος λόγον, Τῷ ἀνδρὶ ὁ ζῆλος παρὰ τοῦ ἑταίρου αὐτοῦ. Καὶ γὰρ οὕτως ἔχει. Οὐχὶ τῷ Αἰγυπτίῳ βασκαίνει ὁ Σκύ θης, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὁμοεθνεῖ ἕκαστος· καὶ ἐν τῷ ὁμοεθνεῖ μέντοι οὐ τοῖς ἀγνοουμένοις φθονεῖ, ἀλλὰ τοῖς συνηθεστάτοις· καὶ τῶν συνήθων τοῖς γείτοσι καὶ ὁμοτέχνοις, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλως οἰκείοις· κἀν τούτοις πά λιν, ἡλικιώταις καὶ συγγενέσι καὶ ἀδελφοῖς. Καὶ ὅλως, ὥσπερ ἡ ἐρυσίβη ἴδιόν ἐστι τοῦ σίτου νόσημα, οὕτως ὁ φθόνος φιλίας ἐστὶν ἀῤῥώστημα.
thought_title: Envy's reach from Joseph to Christ and its remedy in distance
orientation: Basil is preaching against envy, and has just shown how Saul's envy of David grew worse under kindness; now he turns to Joseph's brothers and the Jews' envy of Christ, then urges avoiding close company with envious people.
pass_a_gloss: What beast do they not defeat in the harshness of their ways? What of the wild creatures do they not surpass in savagery? Dogs when fed become tame; lions become manageable when cared for; but envious people are made more savage by acts of care. What made the noble Joseph a slave? Was it not the envy of his brothers? Here indeed it is worth marveling at the unreasonableness of the disease. For fearing the outcome of the dreams, they made their brother a slave, as if a slave would never be bowed down to. And yet if the dreams were true, what device is there that the things foretold should not by all means come to pass? But if the visions of the dreams were false, for what reason do you envy the one who is mistaken? But as it is, by the providence of God their cleverness is turned back upon them. For through the very things by which they thought to hinder the prediction, through these they appeared making a road for its outcome. For if he had not been sold, he would not have come to Egypt, he would not through self-control have fallen into the plots of the licentious woman, he would not have been thrown into prison, he would not have become acquainted with the servants of Pharaoh, nor would he have interpreted the dreams, from which he received rule over Egypt, and because of the famine, when his brothers came to him, he was bowed down to. Pass in your discourse to the greatest envy, and to the one that arose over the greatest things, which came from the madness of the Jews against the Savior. Why was he envied? Because of the wonders. And what were the wonder-workings? Salvation of those in need; the hungry were fed, and the one feeding was warred against; the dead were raised, and the one giving life was envied; demons were driven out, and the one commanding was plotted against; lepers were cleansed, and the lame walked, the deaf heard, and the blind recovered sight, and the benefactor was driven into exile. And finally they handed over to death the one who had granted life, and they scourged the liberator of human beings, and they condemned the judge of the world. Thus the evils of envy went through to all things. And with this one weapon, having begun from the foundation of the world until the consummation of the age, the destroyer of our life, the devil, wounds and casts down all people, the one rejoicing in our destruction, the one who fell through envy, and who casts us down together with himself through the same passion. Wise then was the one who did not permit even dining together with an envious man; from the company at dinner he was speaking about all fellowship in life generally. For just as it is a matter of care for us to put combustible material as far as possible from fire, so it is necessary, as far as possible, to lead friendships away from the company of envious people, making ourselves outside the arrows of envy. For it is not otherwise possible to grapple with envy, unless one has drawn near to it through familiarity. Since indeed according to the word of Solomon, 'A man's envy comes from his companion.' And indeed it is so. The Scythian does not envy the Egyptian, but each person envies the one of his own nation; and among those of the same nation, he does not envy those unknown to him, but those most familiar; and among the familiar, his neighbors and fellow craftsmen, and those otherwise close; and among these again, those of the same age and relatives and brothers. And in general, just as rust is a disease peculiar to grain, so envy is a sickness of friendship.

choices.why: The glossary mandates 'envy' for βασκανία, the same passion as φθόνος.
The glossary mandates 'envious person' for βάσκανος; plural rendered as 'envious people' to avoid the banned 'envious man'.

choices.term: ὁ λυμεὼν τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν διάβολος
choices.english: the destroyer of our life, the devil
choices.why: Keeps the appositional structure of the Greek, where 'the devil' is in apposition to 'the destroyer of our life'; 'the devil' follows the glossary.
The glossary bans 'envious man' for βάσκανος alone, but here the source has the full phrase 'βασκάνῳ ἀνδρί' (envious man), so the literal rendering of the whole phrase is appropriate.
In the Solomon quotation, ζῆλος here denotes the same passion as φθόνος; rendering as 'envy' keeps the homily's consistent terminology and matches the glossary's sense.
Renders the medical metaphor literally; Basil frames envy as a disease of friendship.

bible_refs.note: Τῷ ἀνδρὶ ὁ ζῆλος παρὰ τοῦ ἑταίρου αὐτοῦ (LXX wording; modern translations differ)

pass_b_english: What wild beast do they not surpass in the savagery of their ways? What untamed creature do they not outdo in fierceness? Dogs become gentle when they are fed; lions grow tame when they are cared for; but envious people are made more savage by being cared for. What made the noble Joseph a slave? Was it not the envy of his brothers? And here the unreasonableness of the disease is truly worth admiring. For they feared the fulfillment of the dreams, and so they made their brother a slave—as if a slave could never be bowed down to. Yet if the dreams were true, what device could possibly prevent what had been foretold from coming to pass? And if the visions of the dreams were false, why do you envy a man who is deceived? As it turned out, their cleverness was overturned by God's providence. For by the very means they thought they were blocking the prediction, they were shown to be paving the way for its fulfillment. If he had not been sold, he would not have gone to Egypt; he would not have fallen into the plots of the licentious woman on account of his self-control; he would not have been thrown into prison; he would not have become acquainted with Pharaoh's servants; nor would he have interpreted the dreams, from which he received rule over Egypt and was bowed down to by his brothers when they came to him because of the famine.

Now turn your attention to the greatest envy, the one that arose over the greatest matters—the envy that came from the madness of the Jews against the Savior. Why was He envied? Because of His miracles. And what were His wonder-works? The salvation of those in need. The hungry were fed, and the One who fed them was attacked. The dead were raised, and the One who gave life was envied. Demons were driven out, and the One who commanded them was plotted against. Lepers were cleansed, the lame walked, the deaf heard, the blind received their sight—and the benefactor was hounded away. And in the end they handed over to death the One who granted life, they scourged the liberator of humanity, and they condemned the judge of the world. So the evils of envy ran their course through everything.

With this one weapon, from the foundation of the world to the consummation of the age, the destroyer of our life, the devil, wounds and casts down everyone—he who rejoices in our destruction, who fell through envy and casts us down with himself through the same passion. The man was wise, then, who did not even permit dining with an envious person; from the fellowship at dinner he was speaking about all the sharing of life together. For just as we are careful to store combustible material as far as possible from fire, so we must, as much as we can, keep our friendships away from the company of envious people, placing ourselves outside the arrows of envy. For there is no other way to be entangled with envy except by drawing near to it through intimacy. Since, according to Solomon's word, a man's envy comes from his companion (Proverbs 14:30). And indeed this is how it is. A Scythian does not envy an Egyptian; each person envies his own countryman. And among his own countrymen, he does not envy those he does not know, but those most familiar to him. And among the familiar, his neighbors and fellow craftsmen and those otherwise close to him. And among these again, those of his own age, his relatives, and his brothers. In short, just as rust is a disease peculiar to grain, so envy is a sickness of friendship.

problems.quote: he would not have fallen into the plots of the licentious woman because of his self-control
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἂν διὰ σωφροσύνην ταῖς ἐπιβουλαῖς τῆς ἀκολάστου γυναικὸς περιέπεσεν
problems.why: Joseph fell into the plots BECAUSE OF his chastity, not despite it; his self-control provoked the wife's advances.
problems.fix: he would not have fallen into the plots of the licentious woman on account of his self-control
problems.ruling: διὰ σωφροσύνην means 'because of self-control'; English 'despite' inverts causation. Joseph's chastity provoked her, didn't protect him.

problems.quote: the benefactor was driven into exile
problems.why: 'ἐφυγαδεύετο' is passive/middle of 'drive into exile,' but context shows Christ was not exiled but crucified; English misleads.
problems.fix: the benefactor was hounded away / driven out
problems.ruling: Context is Christ's passion; 'ἐφυγαδεύετο' here means 'driven away/banished,' but 'exile' misleads—Christ was not exiled but put to death.
